newsitem.title: GERMANY: Italy welcome in EMU, Kohl assures Prodi.
newsitem.headline: Italy welcome in EMU, Kohl assures Prodi.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi headed back to Rome late on Thursday night buoyed by assurances from Chancellor Helmut Kohl that Germany wants to see Italy in Europe's planned single currency as soon as possible.

Prodi told reporters after dining with the chancellor that Kohl had given his backing to Italian efforts to get back into the Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) -- a grid designed to prepare countries for merging their currencies.

Prodi said Kohl told him that "from the government side and from him, there would be no obstacles to the re-entry of the lira into the exchange rate mechanism and then into the single European currency."

The warm words from Kohl, the driving force behind European integration, were likely to come as a welcome relief to Prodi after several senior German financial figures expressed doubts about the wisdom of allowing Italy into the currency union.
Prodi also reiterated that he wanted the lira in the ERM by the end of the year.
He said this was the last possible date for the lira's entry into the grid if it was to be part of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) scheduled to begin in January 1999.
The treaty made clear "that any currency had to join the ERM two years before the start of monetary union", Prodi said.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer also said earlier on Thursday in a briefing to Swedish reporters in Frankfurt that the treaty was "very clear" that membership in the exchange rate mechanism was a condition for entry into currency union.
Other countries which do not belong to the ERM, such as Sweden and Britain, have repeatedly said that joining the mechanism was not a prerequisite for joining EMU.
Prodi said Kohl offered backing for Italy's efforts to play a central role in European affairs.
"Germany views very positively a strong Italian presence in European institutions," he said.

Several times this week, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer has emphasised the need for EMU member countries to be capable of long-term financial stability, not just dressing up their budget figures next year to fit the criteria for membership.
The decision on which countries will be founder members of the single currency will be taken in 1998 on the basis of economic data for 1997.
Prodi arrived in Bonn only hours after a board member of Germany's largest commercial bank suggested southern European nations should be excluded from the first wave of EMU to ensure its stability.

"Union must begin with Germany, France, the Benelux nations, Ireland and Austria, but not immediately with the Mediterranean nations," Ulrich Cartellieri of Deutsche Bank AG said in a speech in Luxembourg.
Prodi's visit follows similar talks between Kohl and Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar near Heidelberg on Tuesday which also focused on efforts to qualify for EMU.
The two meetings have fuelled speculation about a possible deal to have Spain and Italy join the commmon European currency soon after 1999, an idea some EU officials favour.
